newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian grain trade eyes Argentine, Kazakh imports.
newsitem.headline: Russian grain trade eyes Argentine, Kazakh imports.

text.p: Moscow's grain trade is casting its eyes as near as Kazakhstan and as far as Argentina in search of cheap supplies to make up for Russia's second poor harvest in a row, trade sources said on Monday.

They also said that while domestic farmers had understated actual 1996 output by as much as 10 percent, Russia still had one of its worst harvests in three decades, with short supplies of high-quality bread-making wheat.

"Of course Argentine wheat is much more attractive right now for Russia than U.S. or Canadian," said a source at a Western commodities house. "But there will be no sudden, big orders -- there will just be some buying here and there."
Trade sources said one Russian firm was considering buying up to 50,000 tonnes of Argentine wheat, but gave no details.
"U.S. wheat is not competitive in terms of price," said a grain marketing source, who said Argentine supplies for delivery to Russia's Far East made more economic sense.
Some European trade sources have wondered whether poor harvests in Eastern Europe, a traditional supplier to Russia, would have an impact on Russian buying patterns.

Arkady Zlochevsky, president of the OGO grain trading company, said Eastern Europe's low output was not a source of worry for Russian importers and that Argentine and Kazakh supplies were more attractive.

A second trade source said Russian importers were not even looking at the possible availability of East European supplies and that Russia had already exported some food wheat and barley to its former Communist bloc neighbours.
Russia's 1996 gross harvest is 74.6 million tonnes, according to preliminary government data -- a figure which most trade sources said did not reflect the truth.

"The actual harvest is at least 1.5 million tonnes and possibly 4.0 million tonnes higher," Zlochevsky said, referring to farmers' traditional propensity to under-report output in order to bolster personal stocks.
A second source said he thought actual output was at least 10 percent higher.
Andrei Sizov of SovEcon Ltd said wheat quality this year was disastrously low.

Traders said it was hard to pin down Russia's grain import needs, citing lower bread consumption and quality, the piecemeal nature of Russian buying and higher, unrecorded imports of foods such as macaroni.
"All of this constitutes what I call the hidden factor in Russia, and it is tough to say what will happen," the marketing source said.
